title: Find Duplicate Emails
problem_statement: Find email addresses that appear more than once in the customers table. Treat emails case-insensitively, so asha@example.com and ASHA@example.com should be treated as the same email.
query:
SELECT
  LOWER(TRIM(email)) AS normalized_email,
  COUNT(*) AS duplicate_count
FROM customers
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email))
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
followup_question: Why do we use GROUP BY and HAVING to find duplicate emails instead of using WHERE alone?
debrief_hint: Group by the normalized email value and filter groups with COUNT(*) > 1. Use LOWER/TRIM when duplicate detection should ignore case and extra spaces.
developer_note: Seed at least one exact duplicate email and one case-variant duplicate email. Also include one NULL email to confirm NULL handling is intentional.

title: Second Highest Order Value
problem_statement: Find the second highest distinct order value from the orders table. If the highest value appears multiple times, it should still count as only the highest distinct value.
query:
SELECT
  MAX(total_amount) AS second_highest_order_value
FROM orders
WHERE total_amount < (
  SELECT MAX(total_amount)
  FROM orders
);
followup_question: Why does this solution use a subquery with MAX(total_amount) instead of simply sorting all orders?
debrief_hint: First find the maximum order value, then find the maximum value that is less than that maximum. This gives the second highest distinct value.
developer_note: Seed tied highest order values and at least one lower value. This checks that the query returns the second highest distinct value, not the second row.

title: Products Above Average Price
problem_statement: Find all products whose price is greater than the average product price. Products with NULL price should not be returned.
query:
SELECT
  product_id,
  product_name,
  price
FROM products
WHERE price > (
  SELECT AVG(price)
  FROM products
  WHERE price IS NOT NULL
);
followup_question: Why is the average price calculated inside a subquery in this problem?
debrief_hint: Use a subquery to calculate the average price, then filter products whose price is greater than that value. NULL prices should not be treated as zero.
developer_note: Include at least one NULL product price and at least one product exactly equal to the average to confirm strict greater-than behavior.

title: Top 3 Products per Category
problem_statement: Find the top 3 revenue-generating products in each category. If products are tied in revenue, they should receive the same rank and all products with rank 3 or better should be included.
query:
WITH product_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    p.category_id,
    c.category_name,
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name,
    SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total_revenue
  FROM products p
  JOIN categories c
    ON p.category_id = c.category_id
  JOIN order_items oi
    ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  GROUP BY
    p.category_id,
    c.category_name,
    p.product_id,
    p.product_name
), ranked_products AS (
  SELECT
    category_id,
    category_name,
    product_id,
    product_name,
    total_revenue,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (
      PARTITION BY category_id
      ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
    ) AS revenue_rank
  FROM product_revenue
)
SELECT
  category_name,
  product_id,
  product_name,
  total_revenue,
  revenue_rank
FROM ranked_products
WHERE revenue_rank <= 3
ORDER BY category_name, revenue_rank, product_id;
followup_question: Why is DENSE_RANK a better fit than ROW_NUMBER when products can have tied revenue?
debrief_hint: Use DENSE_RANK when tied products should share the same rank. A category may return more than 3 rows if there are ties within the top 3 ranks.
developer_note: Seed tied product revenue, including a tie at or near the rank-3 boundary. The expected output may legitimately contain more than 3 products for a category.

title: Customers Who Never Ordered
problem_statement: Find customers who have never placed an order.
query:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.customer_name,
  c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
ORDER BY c.customer_id;
followup_question: Why do we need a LEFT JOIN instead of an INNER JOIN to find customers who never ordered?
debrief_hint: LEFT JOIN keeps all customers. Filtering where the joined order is NULL identifies customers with no matching orders.
developer_note: Seed at least one zero-order customer. Without this edge case, INNER JOIN mistakes may accidentally look correct.

title: Orders with Multiple Items
problem_statement: Find orders that contain more than one item line.
query:
SELECT
  order_id,
  COUNT(*) AS item_count
FROM order_items
GROUP BY order_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
followup_question: Why is HAVING used here instead of WHERE?
debrief_hint: Use GROUP BY to group item lines by order, then HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 to keep only orders with multiple item rows.
developer_note: Seed orders with exactly one item and orders with multiple item rows. Include at least one order with quantity greater than one to distinguish item lines from item quantity.

title: Cumulative Revenue
problem_statement: Calculate daily revenue and cumulative revenue by order date.
query:
WITH daily_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    DATE(order_date) AS revenue_date,
    SUM(total_amount) AS daily_revenue
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY DATE(order_date)
), running_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    revenue_date,
    daily_revenue,
    SUM(daily_revenue) OVER (
      ORDER BY revenue_date
      ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS cumulative_revenue
  FROM daily_revenue
)
SELECT
  revenue_date,
  daily_revenue,
  cumulative_revenue
FROM running_revenue
ORDER BY revenue_date;
followup_question: Why must the window function order by revenue_date when calculating cumulative revenue?
debrief_hint: First aggregate revenue per day. Then use SUM(daily_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY revenue_date) to calculate the running total over time.
developer_note: Seed multiple orders on the same date and multiple dates. Use PostgreSQL date behavior only. Do not validate this query using SQLite for hash generation.

title: Total Revenue per Customer
problem_statement: Find the total revenue generated by each customer who has placed at least one order.
query:
SELECT
  c.customer_id,
  c.customer_name,
  SUM(o.total_amount) AS total_revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o
  ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.customer_name;
followup_question: Why is grouping by customer required when calculating total revenue per customer?
debrief_hint: Join customers with their orders, then group at the customer level and sum order amounts. This version intentionally includes only customers who have placed at least one order.
developer_note: Seed at least one customer with zero orders. That customer should be excluded because the problem is scoped to customers who have placed at least one order.
